artifacts.synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

artifacts.synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

artifacts.title: Schrock et al. v. Philadelphia Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained a complaint against Philadelphia Presbytery for failing to judge and record TE Larry Smith’s stated difference over the continuation of prophecy and tongues beyond the apostolic era. The record showed Presbytery approved Smith’s transfer exam and defeated a motion to find his view out of accord, but it did not categorize that view in Smith’s own words. The SJC remanded for a written statement and Presbytery’s categorical judgment, without undoing Smith’s transfer or deciding whether his view was erroneous.

artifacts.synopsis: Hope Community Church’s Session challenged Presbytery’s requirement that a multi-site congregation eventually particularize its second worship site. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled the requirement, and struck it from the Presbytery Manual because BCO 12-5e specifically entrusts the time and place of worship to the Session, which Presbytery’s general church-enlargement authority could not supersede. The narrow ruling did not resolve broader concerns about multi-site churches or eliminate Presbytery’s review of a second site’s location under BCO 13-9(g).

artifacts.synopsis: Northern California Presbytery adopted an abstract resolution declaring six different views on the diaconate permissible for ministers and Sessions; the SJC sustained the complaints and annulled the resolution, holding that no court may issue binding abstract decrees beyond its proper jurisdictional exercise. A concurring opinion analyzed each of the six diaconal views in detail and set out standards (the GUMP/Kniseley framework) for when diaconal assistant practices are constitutionally permissible.

artifacts.synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the instruction in force. It held that liberty of conscience does not eliminate members’ obligation to obey lawful church injunctions. Here the members had sought the Session’s advice, Presbytery had found no strong presumption of chargeable offenses, and renewed circulation would disturb the church’s peace; under those circumstances, the Session acted within its authority.

artifacts.synopsis: A church member challenged Heritage Presbytery's ruling that the BCO neither expressly nor implicitly requires a congregation to approve changes in a pastor's call, and that it does not require the session to publicize budget details. The SJC held the BCO silent on both points: once the original call and terms are approved, later changes are budgetary and belong to the session under BCO 12-5b; publicizing the budget is prudent but not mandated. The complaint was not sustained; seven commissioners dissented, arguing congregational approval follows by good and necessary consequence.

The Presbytery therefore erred and should have remanded the matter to the Session. No separate merits relief beyond that remand directive appears.

artifacts.synopsis: Three presbyteries asked the General Assembly under BCO 34-1 to assume original jurisdiction over a minister alleged to have allowed women to preach from a church pulpit. The SJC held the requests administratively out of order and did not reach the allegation’s merits. Worship was the Session’s responsibility, so the minister could not be held liable for actions assigned to it; moreover, Tennessee Valley Presbytery had acted on the allegations, defeating BCO 34-1’s refusal-to-act prerequisite. No further proceedings were ordered.

artifacts.synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

artifacts.synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

artifacts.title: Hathaway v. Grace Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A pastor complained that Presbytery upheld his Session’s refusal to give him financial reports prepared for Session members, while also alleging record-transmission, circularization, factual, and constitutional errors. The SJC denied Specifications 1–5 but sustained Specification 6: because the pastor was a Session member, the Session’s authorization made the reports available to him regardless of whether other elders collected copies. His pastoral relationship had ended, however, so the access claim was moot and conferred no present right to the reports. Reasons for Specifications 1–2 were adopted from Case 90-9.

artifacts.synopsis: A complaint challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s approval of proceedings that cleared teaching and ruling elders without properly trying serious public accusations arising from Christ Church’s division. All three specifications were sustained because plea bargaining, dropped charges, and failure to hear necessary witnesses left the accusations unresolved. Presbytery’s action was annulled and de novo trials produced mixed convictions and acquittals. Harold Burkhart received six months’ suspension, Douglas McCready an admonition, and six former ruling elders three-month suspensions. The decision stressed taking such conflicts to Presbytery or judicial process rather than the congregation.

artifacts.synopsis: Philadelphia Presbytery treated a letter as a complaint although it had not first been filed with the Session, judged the Session without proper process, and asked its clerk to facilitate membership transfers despite the Session's authority over dismissal letters. Those and a constitutional-limits specification were sustained; claims that Presbytery neglected underlying questions and acted for the Session were not. The March 12 actions were annulled, specified language expunged, and Presbytery directed to adopt safeguards for constitutional inquiries and review relevant church-law materials.
